newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-ASTONISHING "CRAZY GANG" CONTINUE TO DEFY LOGIC.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ASTONISHING "CRAZY GANG" CONTINUE TO DEFY LOGIC.

text.p: Wimbledon don't play on their own ground, they have the lowest gates in the English premier league and bizarrely considered moving to Dublin.

But despite all that -- and a lot more besides -- the club that revels in the nickname the "Crazy Gang" were level on points with Arsenal and Newcastle at the top of arguably the toughest league in the world on Saturday night.
And only a slightly inferior goal difference than Arsenal's meant the Gunners were top and Wimbledon second.
On Saturday afternoon, manager Joe Kinnear's men demolished Ruud Gullit's Chelsea 4-2 at Stamford Bridge for their seventh successive league victory.
Their performance was praised by player-manager Gullit -- no bad judge of a good team -- and was far removed from their old style kick-it-and-see-what-happens philosophy.
Since being voted into the English League 19 years ago, Wimbledon have risen through the divisions, won the F.A. Cup and never been relegated from the top division since reaching it in 1986.
Just over 10 years ago they briefly topped the old first division -- and the win at Chelsea to go second is their highest position since then.
But their football today is very different from the way they played in the past.

As Gullit said: "Wimbledon were excellent in that they paid attention to the small details. They moved the ball around intelligently, they ran and worked for one another. They showed a lot of discipline and are hard to beat."

Wimbledon revel in doing things differently and as Kinnear says: "We can't compete with the Manchester Uniteds and the Newcastles in terms of money, but we can match their team spirit, their commitment and their ambition on the field where it matters.
"We don't go out to intimidate anyone, but if we've got the ghetto-blaster going full tilt in the dressing room -- well, the opposition know we're there."
Wimbledon skipper Vinnie Jones, former hod-carrier, aspiring actor and a recent guest speaker at the Oxford Union, summed up the current feeling in the Wimbledon camp.
"The spirit is better than it has ever been and the message in the dressing room before the game was that we mustn't let the bubble burst in a bad way by getting heavily beaten.
"We've got to do the things we're good at and as long as we keep doing them we're a match for any team in the country."
Wimbledon never do things by halves. At the start of the season they lost three straight matches without scoring a goal and were most people's favourites to go down.
Since then they have won seven straight league matches with a goal tally of 20-5, and on Saturday night bookmakers William Hill slashed their championship odds from 100-1 to 50-1.

Behind the scenes Wimbledon are as unorthodox as they have been on it. They ground-share with Crystal Palace, five miles from their old home ground where the record attendance of 18,000 was set in the 1930s against a team of sailors from HMS Victory.

They train in a public park next to a major road and are bankrolled by their benevolent Lebanese millionaire owner Sam Hammam, who often shuns the directors' box at matches to stand on the touchline cheering the team on, wearing a flat cap and an anorak.
They have to produce their own stars to survive and their Football-in-the-Community scheme is regarded as the best in the country.

Thousands of children are enrolled as Crazy Gang members and are trained by the club during school holidays. The search never ends for the uncut schoolboy soccer diamonds who may one day be worth millions.

Their average gate is around 9,000 and the struggle to survive is so tough the club even considered the idea of moving to Dublin where potential support is far greater, but that plan now appears dead and buried. Instead the club are engaged in a fight with their local council to move back to the Wimbledon area.
Kinnear, who had a "normal" career with Tottenham and as an Ireland international in the 1960s and 70s, has shrewdly blended all of the club's wilder characteristics with pragmatic footballing sense.
But a sense of humour is never far away.
"The only reason Sam came on to the touchline today after the fourth goal went in was to tell the players: `don't score any more goals because I can't afford the bonuses'."
Kinnear says that Wimbledon's realistic targets this season could be winning a cup and finishing high enough to qualify for Europe.
"I've talked before about aiming to finish in the top eight and winning a place in Europe next season and now we're starting to believe that that's possible," he said.
With Wimbledon, just about anything is.
